entries.ffcf0749e9ef5419bf1c1f2aec61967874d39620: <div sID="gen13135" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="139" osisID="Ps.139" sID="Ps.139"/> <div eID="gen13135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13136" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13137" type="x-p"/> Some of the Jewish doctors are of opinion that this is the most excellent of all the psalms of David; and a very pious devout meditation it is upon the doctrine of God's omniscience, which we should therefore have our hearts fixed upon and filled with in singing this psalm. I. This doctrine is here asserted, and fully laid down, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. It is confirmed by two arguments:—1. God is every where present; therefore he knows all, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.7-Ps.139.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. 2. He made us, therefore he knows us, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. III. Some inferences are drawn from this doctrine. 1. It may fill us with pleasing admiration of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17-Ps.139.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. 2. With a holy dread and detestation of sin and sinners, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19-Ps.139.22">ver. 19-22</reference>. 3. With a holy satisfaction in our own integrity, concerning which we may appeal to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23-Ps.139.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>. This great and self-evident truth, That God knows our hearts, and the hearts of all the children of men, if we did but mix faith with it and seriously consider it and apply it, would have a great influence upon our holiness and upon our comfort.
entries.38efdafd4f3fa8c12a0290a8f59835e6f92a41fd: <div eID="gen13137" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13136" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Omniscience of God.</title> <div sID="gen13138" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou hast searched me, and known <hi type="italic">me.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted <hi type="italic">with</hi> all my ways. <hi type="super">4</hi> For <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not a word in my tongue, <hi type="italic">but,</hi> lo, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou knowest it altogether. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me. 6 <hi type="italic">Such</hi> knowledge <hi type="italic">is</hi> too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot <hi type="italic">attain</hi> unto it. <div eID="gen13138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13139" type="x-p"/> David here lays down this great doctrine, That the God with whom we have to do has a perfect knowledge of us, and that all the motions and actions both of our inward and of our outward man are naked and open before him. <div eID="gen13139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13140" type="x-p"/> I. He lays down this doctrine in the way of an address to God; he says it to him, acknowledging it to him, and giving him the glory of it. Divine truths look fully as well when they are prayed over as when they are preached over, and much better than when they are disputed over. When we speak of God to him himself we shall find ourselves concerned to speak with the utmost degree both of sincerity and reverence, which will be likely to make the impressions the deeper. <div eID="gen13140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13141" type="x-p"/> II. He lays it down in a way of application to himself, not, "Thou hast known <hi type="italic">all,</hi>" but, "Thou hast known <hi type="italic">me;</hi> that is it which I am most concerned to believe and which it will be most profitable for me to consider." <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we know these things for our good when we know them <hi type="italic">for ourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.27">Job v. 27</reference>. When we acknowledge, "Lord, all souls are thine," we must add, "My soul is thine; thou that hatest all sin hatest my sin; thou that art good to all, good to Israel, art good to me." So here, "<hi type="italic">Thou hast searched me, and known me;</hi> known me as thoroughly as we know that which we have most diligently and exactly searched into." David was a king, and <hi type="italic">the hearts of kings are unsearchable</hi> to their subjects (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Prov. xxv. 3</reference>), but they are not so to their Sovereign. <div eID="gen13141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13142" type="x-p"/> III. He descends to particulars: "Thou knowest me wherever I am and whatever I am doing, me and all that belongs to me." 1. "<hi type="italic">Thou knowest</hi> me and all my motions, <hi type="italic">my down-sitting</hi> to rest, <hi type="italic">my up-rising</hi> to work, with what temper of mind I compose myself when I sit down and stir up myself when I rise up, what my soul reposes itself in as its stay and support, what it aims at and reaches towards as its felicity and end. Thou knowest me when I come home, how I walk before my house, and when I go abroad, on what errands I go." 2. "Thou knowest all my imaginations. Nothing is more close and quick than thought; it is always unknown to others; it is often unobserved by ourselves, and yet <hi type="italic">thou understandest my thought afar off.</hi> Though my thoughts be ever so foreign and distant from one another, thou understandest the chain of them, and canst make out their connexion, when so many of them slip my notice that I myself cannot." Or, "<hi type="italic">Thou understandest them afar off,</hi> even before I think them, and long after I have thought them and have myself forgotten them." Or, "<hi type="italic">Thou understandest them from afar;</hi> from the height of heaven thou seest into the depths of the heart," <reference osisRef="Ps.33.14">Ps. xxxiii. 14</reference>. 3. "Thou knowest me and all my designs and undertakings; <hi type="italic">thou compassest</hi> every particular <hi type="italic">path; thou siftest</hi> (or <hi type="italic">winnowest</hi>) <hi type="italic">my path</hi>" (so some), "so as thoroughly to distinguish between the good and evil of what I do," as by sifting we separate between the corn and the chaff. All our actions are ventilated by the judgment of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Ps. xvii. 3</reference>. God takes notice of every step we take, every right step and every by-step. He is <hi type="italic">acquainted with all</hi> our <hi type="italic">ways,</hi> intimately acquainted with them; he knows what rule we walk by, what end we walk towards, what company we walk with. 4. "<hi type="italic">Thou knowest</hi> me in all my retirements; thou knowest <hi type="italic">my lying down;</hi> when I am withdrawn from all company, and am reflecting upon what has passed all day and composing myself to rest, thou knowest what I have in my heart and with what thought I go to bed." 5. "Thou knowest me, and all I say (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is not a word in my tongue,</hi> not a vain word, nor a good word, <hi type="italic">but thou knowest it altogether,</hi> knowest what it meant, from what thought it came, and with what design it was uttered. There is not a word at my tongue's end, ready to be spoken, yet checked and kept in, but thou knowest it." <hi type="italic">When there is not a word in my tongue, O Lord! thou knowest all</hi> (so some read it); for thoughts are words to God. 6. "Thou knowest me in every part of me: <hi type="italic">Thou hast beset me behind and before,</hi> so that, go which way I will, I am under thy eye and cannot possibly escape it. Thou hast <hi type="italic">laid thy hand upon me,</hi> and I can not run away from thee." Wherever we are we are under the eye and hand of God. perhaps it is an allusion to the physician's laying his hand upon his patient to feel how his pulse beats or what temper he is in. God knows us as we know not only what we see, but what we feel and have our hands upon. <hi type="italic">All his saints are in his hand.</hi> <div eID="gen13142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13143" type="x-p"/> IV. He speaks of it with admiration (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is too wonderful for me; it is high.</hi> 1. "Thou hast such a knowledge of me as I have not of myself, nor can have. I cannot take notice of all my own thoughts, nor make such a judgment of myself as thou makest of me." 2. "It is such a knowledge as I cannot comprehend, much less describe. That thou knowest all things I am sure, but how I cannot tell." We cannot by searching find out how God searches and finds out us; nor do we know how we are known.
entries.881bb22705724ca6287a8428a7022604e7017fce: <div eID="gen13143" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Omniscience of God.</title> <div sID="gen13144" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? <hi type="super">8</hi> If I ascend up into heaven, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou <hi type="italic">art there.</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> I take the wings of the morning, <hi type="italic">and</hi> dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; <hi type="super">10</hi> Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me. <hi type="super">11</hi> If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me. <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light <hi type="italic">are</hi> both alike <hi type="italic">to thee.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. <hi type="super">14</hi> I will praise thee; for I am fearfully <hi type="italic">and</hi> wonderfully made: marvellous <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy works; and <hi type="italic">that</hi> my soul knoweth right well. <hi type="super">15</hi> My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, <hi type="italic">and</hi> curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all <hi type="italic">my members</hi> were written, <hi type="italic">which</hi> in continuance were fashioned, when <hi type="italic">as yet there was</hi> none of them. <div eID="gen13144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13145" type="x-p"/> It is of great use to us to know the certainty of the things wherein we have been instructed, that we may not only believe them, but be able to tell why we believe them, and to give a reason of the hope that is in us. David is sure that God perfectly knows him and all his ways, <div eID="gen13145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13146" type="x-p"/> I. Because he is always under his eye. If God is omnipresent, he must needs be omniscient; but he is omnipresent; this supposes the infinite and immensity of his being, from which follows the ubiquity of his presence; heaven and earth include the whole creation, and the Creator fills both (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.24">Jer. xxiii. 24</reference>); he not only knows both, and governs both, but he fills both. Every part of the creation is under God's intuition and influence. David here acknowledges this also with application and sees himself thus open before God. <div eID="gen13146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13147" type="x-p"/> 1. No flight can remove us out of God's presence: "<hi type="italic">Whither shall I go from thy Spirit, from thy presence,</hi> that is, from thy spiritual presence, from thyself, who art a Spirit?" <hi type="italic">God is a Spirit,</hi> and therefore it is folly to think that because we cannot see him he cannot see us: <hi type="italic">Whither shall I flee from thy presence?</hi> Not that he desired to go away from God; no, he desired nothing more than to be near him; but he only puts the case, "Suppose I should be so foolish as to think of getting out of thy sight, that I might shake off the awe of thee, suppose I should think of revolting from my obedience to thee, or of disowning a dependence on thee and of shifting for myself, alas! whither can I go?" A heathen could say, <hi type="italic">Quocunque te flexeris, ibi Deum videbis occurrentem tibi—Whithersoever thou turnest thyself, thou wilt see God meeting thee.</hi> Seneca. He specifies the most remote and distant places, and counts upon meeting God in them. (1.) In heaven: "<hi type="italic">If I ascend</hi> thither, as I hope to do shortly, <hi type="italic">thou art there,</hi> and it will be my eternal bliss to be with thee there." Heaven is a vast large place, replenished with an innumerable company, and yet there is no escaping God's eye there, in any corner, or in any crowd. The inhabitants of that world have as necessary a dependence upon God, and lie as open to his strict scrutiny, as the inhabitants of this. (2.) <hi type="italic">In hell</hi>—in <hi type="italic">Sheol,</hi> which may be understood of the depth of the earth, the very centre of it. Should we dig as deep as we can under ground, and think to hide ourselves there, we should be mistaken; God knows that path which the vulture's eye never saw, and to him the earth is all surface. Or it may be understood of the state of the dead. When we are removed out of the sight of all living, yet not out of the sight of the living God; from his eye we cannot hide ourselves in the grave. Or it maybe understood of the place of the damned: <hi type="italic">If I make my bed in hell</hi> (an uncomfortable place to make a bed in, where there is no rest day or night, yet thousands will make their bed for ever in those flames), <hi type="italic">behold, thou art there,</hi> in thy power and justice. God's wrath is the fire which will there burn everlastingly, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>. (3.) In the remotest corners of this world: "<hi type="italic">If I take the wings of the morning,</hi> the rays of the morning-light (called the wings of the sun, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">Mal. iv. 2</reference>), than which nothing more swift, and flee upon them to <hi type="italic">the uttermost parts of the sea,</hi> or of the earth (<reference osisRef="Job.38.12-Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 12, 13</reference>), should I flee to the most distant and obscure islands (the <hi type="italic">ultima Thule,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Terra incognita</hi>), I should find thee there; <hi type="italic">there shall thy hand lead me,</hi> as far as I go, <hi type="italic">and thy right hand hold me,</hi> that I can go no further, that I cannot go out of thy reach." God soon arrested Jonah when <hi type="italic">he fled to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen13147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13148" type="x-p"/> 2. No veil can hide us from God's eye, no, not that of the thickest darkness, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.11-Ps.139.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. "<hi type="italic">If I say,</hi> Yet <hi type="italic">the darkness shall cover me,</hi> when nothing else will, alas! I find myself deceived; the curtains of the evening will stand me in no more stead than the wings of the morning; <hi type="italic">even the night shall be light about me.</hi> That which often favours the escape of a pursued criminal, and the retreat of a beaten army, will do me no kindness in fleeing from them." When God divided between the light and darkness it was with a reservation of this prerogative, that to himself <hi type="italic">the darkness and the light</hi> should still be <hi type="italic">both alike. "The darkness</hi> darkeneth <hi type="italic">not from thee,</hi> for there is no darkness nor shadow of death where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves." No hypocritical mask or disguise, how specious soever, can save any person or action from appearing in a true light before God. Secret haunts of sin are as open before God as the most open and barefaced villanies. <div eID="gen13148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13149" type="x-p"/> II. Because he is the work of his hands. He that framed the engine knows all the motions of it. God made us, and therefore no doubt he knows us; he saw us when we were in the forming, and can we be hidden from him now that we are formed? This argument he insists upon (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.16">v. 13-16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast possessed my reins;</hi> thou art Master of my most secret thoughts and intentions, and the innermost recesses of my soul; thou not only knowest, but governest, them, as we do that which we have possession of; and the possession thou hast of my reins is a rightful possession, <hi type="italic">for thou coveredst me in my mother's womb,</hi> that is, thou madest me (<reference osisRef="Job.10.11">Job x. 11</reference>), thou madest me in secret. The soul is concealed from all about us. <hi type="italic">Who knows the things of a man, save the spirit of a man?</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 11</reference>. Hence we read of <hi type="italic">the hidden man of the heart.</hi> But it was God himself that thus covered us, and therefore he can, when he pleases, discover us; when he hid us from all the world he did not intend to hide us from himself. Concerning the formation of man, of each of us, <div eID="gen13149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13150" type="x-p"/> 1. The glory of it is here given to God, entirely to him; <hi type="italic">for it is he that has made us and not we ourselves. "I will praise thee,</hi> the author of my being; my parents were only the instruments of it." It was done, (1.) Under the divine inspection: <hi type="italic">My substance,</hi> when hid in the womb, nay, when it was yet but <hi type="italic">in fieri—in the forming,</hi> an unshapen embryo, <hi type="italic">was not hidden from thee; thy eyes did see my substance.</hi> (2.) By the divine operation. As the eye of God saw us then, so his hand wrought us; we were his work. (3.) According to the divine model: <hi type="italic">In thy book all my members were written.</hi> Eternal wisdom formed the plan, and by that almighty power raised the noble structure. <div eID="gen13150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13151" type="x-p"/> 2. Glorious things are here said concerning it. The generation of man is to be considered with the same pious veneration as his creation at first. Consider it, (1.) As a great marvel, a great miracle we might call it, but that it is done in the ordinary course of nature. We are <hi type="italic">fearfully and wonderfully made;</hi> we may justly be astonished at the admirable contrivance of these living temples, the composition of every part, and the harmony of all together. (2.) As a great mystery, a mystery of nature: <hi type="italic">My soul knows right well</hi> that it is marvellous, but how to describe it for any one else I know not; for <hi type="italic">I was made in secret, and curiously wrought</hi> in the womb as <hi type="italic">in the lowest parts of the earth,</hi> so privately, and so far out of sight. (3.) As a great mercy, that all our members <hi type="italic">in continuance were fashioned,</hi> according as they were written in the book of God's wise counsel, <hi type="italic">when as yet there was none of them;</hi> or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">and none of them was left out.</hi> If any of our members had been wanting in God's book, they would have been wanting in our bodies, but, through his goodness, we have all our limbs and sense, the want of any of which might have made us burdens to ourselves. See what reason we have then to praise God for our creation, and to conclude that he who saw our substance when it was unfashioned sees it now that it is fashioned.
entries.d31604624cb0d28f4e2b4c694a06b27bca414088: <div eID="gen13151" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Omniscience of God.</title> <div sID="gen13152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them! <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee. <hi type="super">19</hi> Surely thou wilt slay the wicked, O God: depart from me therefore, ye bloody men. <hi type="super">20</hi> For they speak against thee wickedly, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thine enemies take <hi type="italic">thy name</hi> in vain. <hi type="super">21</hi> Do not I hate them, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? <hi type="super">22</hi> I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies. <hi type="super">23</hi> Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: <hi type="super">24</hi> And see if <hi type="italic">there be any</hi> wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. <div eID="gen13152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13153" type="x-p"/> Here the psalmist makes application of the doctrine of God's omniscience, divers ways. <div eID="gen13153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13154" type="x-p"/> I. He acknowledges, with wonder and thankfulness, the care God had taken of him all his days, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17-Ps.139.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. God, who knew him, thought of him, and his thoughts towards him were thoughts of love, <hi type="italic">thoughts of good, and not of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>. God's omniscience, which might justly have watched over us to do us hurt, has been employed for us, and has watched over us to do us good, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.28">Jer. xxxi. 28</reference>. God's counsels concerning us and our welfare have been, 1. Precious to admiration: <hi type="italic">How precious</hi> are they! They are deep in themselves, such as cannot possibly be fathomed and comprehended. Providence has had a vast reach in its dispensations concerning us, and has brought things about for our good quite beyond our contrivance and foresight. They are dear to us; we must think of them with a great deal of reverence, and yet with pleasure and thankfulness. Our thoughts concerning God must be delightful to us, above any other thoughts. 2. Numerous to admiration: <hi type="italic">How great is the sum of them!</hi> We cannot conceive how many God's kind counsels have been concerning us, how many good turns he has done us, and what variety of mercies we have received from him. <hi type="italic">If</hi> we would <hi type="italic">count them,</hi> the heads of them, much more the particulars of them, <hi type="italic">they are more in number than the sand,</hi> and yet every one great and very considerable, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Ps. xl. 5</reference>. We cannot conceive the multitude of God's compassions, which are all new every morning. 3. Constant at all times: "<hi type="italic">When I awake,</hi> every morning, <hi type="italic">I am still with thee,</hi> under thy eye and care, safe and easy under thy protection." This bespeaks also the continual devout sense David had of the eye of God upon him: <hi type="italic">When I awake I am with thee,</hi> in my thoughts; and it would help to keep us in the fear of the Lord all the day long if, when we awake in the morning, our first thoughts were of him and we did then set him before us. <div eID="gen13154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13155" type="x-p"/> II. He concludes from this doctrine that ruin will certainly be the end of sinners. God knows all the wickedness of the wicked, and therefore he will reckon for it: "<hi type="italic">Surely thou wilt slay the wicked, O God!</hi> for all their wickedness is open before thee, however it may be artfully disguised and coloured over, to hide it from the eye of the world. However thou suffer them to prosper for a while, <hi type="italic">surely thou wilt slay</hi> them at last." Now observe, 1. The reason why God will punish them, because they daringly affront him and set him at defiance (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">They speak against thee wickedly;</hi> they <hi type="italic">set their mouth against the heavens</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Ps. lxxiii. 9</reference>), and shall be called to account for the hard speeches they have <hi type="italic">spoken against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. They are his <hi type="italic">enemies,</hi> and declare their enmity by <hi type="italic">taking his name in vain,</hi> as we show our contempt of a man if we make a by-word of his name, and never mention him but in a way of jest and banter. Those that profane the sacred forms of swearing or praying by using them in an impertinent irreverent manner take God's name in vain, and thereby show themselves enemies to him. Some make it to be a description of hypocrites: "They speak of thee for mischief; they talk of God, pretending to piety, but it is with some ill design, for a cloak of maliciousness; and, being enemies to God, while they pretend friendship, they <hi type="italic">take</hi> his <hi type="italic">name in vain;</hi> they swear falsely." 2. The use David makes of this prospect which he has of the ruin of the wicked. (1.) He defies them: "<hi type="italic">Depart from me, you bloody men;</hi> you shall not debauch me, for I will not admit your friendship nor have fellowship with you; and you cannot destroy me, for, being under God's protection, he shall force you to depart from me." (2.) He detests them (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.21-Ps.139.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): "Lord, thou knowest the heart, and canst witness for me; <hi type="italic">do not I hate those that hate thee,</hi> and for that reason, because they hate thee? I hate them because I love thee, and hate to see such affronts and indignities put upon thy blessed name. <hi type="italic">Am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee,</hi> grieved to see their rebellion and to foresee their ruin, which it will certainly end in?" Note, Sin is hated, and sinners are lamented, by all that fear God. "<hi type="italic">I hate them</hi>" (that is, "<hi type="italic">I hate the work of them that turn aside,</hi>" as he explains himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Ps. ci. 3</reference>) "<hi type="italic">with a</hi> sincere and <hi type="italic">perfect hatred; I count those</hi> that are enemies to God as enemies to me, and will not have any intimacy with them," <reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Ps. lxix. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen13155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13156" type="x-p"/> III. He appeals to God concerning his sincerity, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23-Ps.139.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. 1. He desires that as far as he was in the wrong God would discover it to him. Those that are upright can take comfort in God's omniscience as a witness of their uprightness, and can with a humble confidence beg of him to search and try them, to discover them to themselves (for a good man desires to know the worst of himself) and to discover them to others. He that means honestly could wish he had a window in his breast that any man may look into his heart: "Lord, I hope I am not in a wicked way, but <hi type="italic">see if there be any wicked way in me,</hi> any corrupt inclination remaining; let me see it; and root it out of me, for I do not allow it." 2. He desires that, as far as he was in the right, he might be forwarded in it, which he that knows the heart knows how to do effectually: <hi type="italic">Lead me in the way everlasting.</hi> Note, (1.) The way of godliness is an everlasting way; it is everlastingly true and good, pleasing to God and profitable to us, and will end in everlasting life. <hi type="italic">It is the way of antiquity</hi> (so some), <hi type="italic">the good old way.</hi> (2.) All the saints desire to be kept and led in this way, that they may not miss it, turn out of it, nor tire in it.  <chapter eID="Ps.139"/> <div eID="gen13156" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ecb904e1f0c82027c18e2e7782e4ae0600030cf: <chapter n="139" osisID="Ps.139" sID="Ps.139"/><div eID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7084"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 139</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.24">Psa 139:1-24</reference>. After presenting the sublime doctrines of God's omnipresence and omniscience, the Psalmist appeals to Him, avowing his innocence, his abhorrence of the wicked, and his ready submission to the closest scrutiny. Admonition to the wicked and comfort to the pious are alike implied inferences from these doctrines.</title> <div sID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.139"/>

entries.3efaa6438e5f4ca9029803b4ea0b6ca105e5255d: <div eID="gen23309" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23312" type="x-p"/> A fine account of the omniscience of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.1-Psa.139.6">Psa 139:1-6</reference>; of his omnipresence, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.7-Psa.139.12">Psa 139:7-12</reference>; of his power and providence <reference osisRef="Psa.139.13-Psa.139.16">Psa 139:13-16</reference>. The excellence of his purposes, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.18">Psa 139:18</reference>. His opposition to the wicked, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference>; with whom the godly can have no fellowship, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.21">Psa 139:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.22">Psa 139:22</reference>. <div eID="gen23312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23313" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm in the Hebrew is, To the chief Musician, or, To the Conqueror, A Psalm of David. The Versions in general follow the Hebrew. And yet, notwithstanding these testimonies, there appears internal evidence that the Psalm was not written by David, but during or after the time of the captivity, as there are several Chaldaisms in it. See <reference osisRef="Psa.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.7">Psa 139:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.9">Psa 139:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference>, collated with <reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Dan 2:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.30">Dan 2:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">Dan 7:28</reference>; some of these shall be noticed in their proper places. <div eID="gen23313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23314" type="x-p"/> As to the author, he is unknown; for it does not appear to have been the work of David. The composition is worthy of him, but the language appears to be lower than his time. <div eID="gen23314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23315" type="x-p"/> Concerning the occasion, there are many conjectures which I need not repeat, because I believe them unfounded. It is most probable that it was written on no particular occasion, but is a moral lesson on the wisdom, presence, providence, and justice of God, without any reference to any circumstance in the life of David, or in the history of the Jews. <div eID="gen23315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23316" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is very sublime; the sentiments are grand, the style in general highly elevated, and the images various and impressive. The first part especially, that contains so fine a description of the wisdom and knowledge of God, is inimitable. <div eID="gen23316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23317" type="x-p"/> Bishop Horsley's account of this Psalm is as follows: - "In the first twelve verses of this Psalm the author celebrates God's perfect knowledge of man's thoughts and actions; and the reason of this wonderful knowledge, viz., that God is the Maker of man. Hence the psalmist proceeds, in the four following verses, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.13-Psa.139.16">Psa 139:13-16</reference>, to magnify God as ordaining and superintending the formation of his body in the womb. In the 17th and 18th (<reference osisRef="Psa.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.139.18">Psa 139:18</reference>) he acknowledges God's providential care of him in every moment of his life; and in the remainder of the Psalm implores God's aid against impious and cruel enemies, professing his own attachment to God's service, that is, to the true religion, and appealing to the Searcher of hearts himself for the truth of his professions." <div eID="gen23317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> The composition, for the purity and justness of religious sentiment, and for the force and beauty of the images, is certainly in the very first and best style. And yet the frequent Chaldaisms of the diction argue no very high antiquity. <div eID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23319" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23320" type="x-p"/> O Lord, thou hast searched me - חקרתני chakartani; thou hast investigated me; thou hast thoroughly acquainted thyself with my whole soul and conduct.
entries.a6b69f85e270673805fa640f2d3f6ee5b6aa8353: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23321" type="x-p"/> My downsitting and mine uprising - Even these inconsiderable and casual things are under thy continual notice. I cannot so much as take a seat, or leave it, without being marked by thee. <div eID="gen23321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23322" type="x-p"/> Thou understandest my thought - לרעי lerei, "my cogitation." This word is Chaldee, see <reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Dan 2:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.30">Dan 2:30</reference>. <div eID="gen23322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23323" type="x-p"/> Afar off - While the figment is forming that shall produce them.
entries.e0e1dcc7dc0b4e94769ece4ba21d788f14ce771c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23324" type="x-p"/> Thou compassest my path - זרית zeritha thou dost winnow, ventilate, or sift my path; and my lying down, רבעי ribi, my lair, my bed. <div eID="gen23324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23325" type="x-p"/> And art acquainted - Thou treasurest up. This is the import of סכן sachan. Thou hast the whole number of my ways, and the steps I took in them.
entries.3e98ba76e6114ba0c9928f0ad59735012eee9401: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23326" type="x-p"/> There is not a word in my tongue - Although (כי ki) there be not a word in my tongue, behold O Jehovah, thou knowest the whole of it, that is, thou knowest all my words before they are uttered as thou knowest all my thoughts while as yet they are unformed.
entries.d1f3589519f08d1baa9158ca2992cf671729eaec: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23327" type="x-p"/> Thou hast beset me behind and before - אחור וקדם צרתני achor vekodam tsartani, "The hereafter and the past, thou hast formed me." I think Bishop Horsley's emendation here is just, uniting the two verses together. "Behold thou, O Jehovah, knowest the whole, the hereafter and the past. Thou hast formed me, and laid thy hand upon me."
entries.8c345e40731a05b9a0c1adab8b5449cd59fc315b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23328" type="x-p"/> Such knowledge is too wonderful - I think, with Kennicott, that פלאיה דעת pelaiah daath should be read פלאי הדעת peli haddaath, "This knowledge," ממני mimmenni, "is beyond or above me." This change is made by taking the ה he from the end of פלאיה pelaiah, which is really no word, and joining it with דעת daath; which, by giving it an article, makes it demonstrative, הדעת haddaath, "This knowledge." This kind of knowledye, God's knowledge, that takes in all things, and their reasons, essences, tendencies, and issues, is far beyond me.
entries.7a44c4e82acb94b99d6b48667a38c04ee0c59eba: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23329" type="x-p"/> Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? - Surely רוח ruach in this sense must be taken personally, it certainly cannot mean either breath or wind; to render it so would make the passage ridiculous. <div eID="gen23329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23330" type="x-p"/> From thy presence? - מפניך mippaneycha, "from thy faces." Why do we meet with this word so frequently in the plural number, when applied to God? And why have we his Spirit, and his appearances or faces, both here? A Trinitarian would at once say, "The plurality of persons in the Godhead is intended;" and who can prove that he is mistaken?
entries.14231b8cb149c298562f8976427cf6257cf0e5e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23331" type="x-p"/> If I ascend - Thou art in heaven, in thy glory; in hell, in thy vindictive justice; and in all parts or earth, water, space, place, or vacuity, by thy omnipresence. Wherever I am, there art thou; and where I cannot be, thou art there. Thou fillest the heavens and the earth.
entries.b865de954a6d99a7bbed6603cd8fa41514b17cd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> Surely the darkness shall cover me - Should I suppose that this would serve to screen me, immediately this darkness is turned into light.
entries.a73f3b3aec2fd803e4687f0c5e7a42ae21676efd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23333" type="x-p"/> Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee - Darkness and light, ignorance and knowledge, are things that stand in relation to us; God sees equally in darkness as in light; and knows as perfectly, however man is enveloped in ignorance, as if all were intellectual brightness. What is to us hidden by darkness, or unknown through ignorance, is perfectly seen and known by God; because he is all sight, all hearing, all feeling, all soul, all spirit - all in All, and infinite in himself. He lends to every thing; receives nothing from any thing. Though his essence be unimpartible, yet his influence is diffusible through time and through eternity. Thus God makes himself known, seen, heard, felt; yet, in the infinity of his essence, neither angel, nor spirit, nor man can see him; nor can any creature comprehend him, or form any idea of the mode of his existence. And yet vain man would be wise, and ascertain his foreknowledge, eternal purposes, infinite decrees, with all operations of infinite love and infinite hatred, and their objects specifically and nominally, from all eternity, as if himself had possessed a being and powers co-extensive with the Deity! O ye wise fools! Jehovah, the fountain of eternal perfection and love, is as unlike your creeds as he is unlike yourselves, forgers of doctrines to prove that Ithe source of infinite benevolence is a streamlet of capricious love to thousands, while he is an overflowing, eternal, and irresistible tide of hatred to millions of millions both of angels and men! The antiproof of such doctrines is this: he bears with such blasphemies, and does not consume their abettors. "But nobody holds these doctrines." Then I have written against nobody; and have only to add the prayer, May no such doctrines ever disgrace the page of history; or farther dishonor, as they have done, the annals of the Church!
entries.398083543a32d4a1dc52e01ec83d81654e9c786e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23334" type="x-p"/> Thou hast possessed my reins - As the Hebrews believed that the reins were the first part of the human fetus that is formed, it may here mean, thou hast laid the foundation of my being.
entries.3a4c396781b6962ff25fe324303ffb9d1c36fd03: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23335" type="x-p"/> I am fearfully and wonderfully made - The texture of the human body is the most complicated and curious that can be conceived. It is, indeed, wonderfully made; and it is withal so exquisitely nice and delicate, that the slightest accident may impair or destroy in a moment some of those parts essentially necessary to the continuance of life; therefore, we are fearfully made. And God has done so to show us our frailty, that we should walk with death, keeping life in view; and feel the necessity of depending on the all-wise and continual superintending care and providence of God.
entries.25f62d4a8c1621ccf00f6fef0a251d1d6e6539c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23336" type="x-p"/> My substance was not hid from thee - עצמי atsmi, my bones or skeleton. <div eID="gen23336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23337" type="x-p"/> Curiously wrought - רקמתי rukkamti, embroidered, made of needlework. These two words, says Bishop Horsley, describe the two principal parts of which the human body is composed; the bony skeleton, the foundation of the whole; and the external covering of muscular flesh, tendons, veins, arteries, nerves, and skin; a curious web of fibres. On this passage Bishop Lowth has some excellent observations: "In that most perfect hymn, where the immensity of the omnipresent Deity, and the admirable wisdom of the Divine Artificer in framing the human body, are celebrated, the poet uses a remarkable metaphor, drawn from the nicest tapestry work: - <div eID="gen23337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23338" type="x-p"/> When I was formed in secret; <div eID="gen23338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23339" type="x-p"/> When I was wrought, as with a needle, in the lowest parts of the earth. "He who remarks this, (but the man who consults Versions only will hardly remark it), and at the same time reflects upon the wonderful composition of the human body, the various implication of veins, arteries, fibres, membranes, and the 'inexplicable texture' of the whole frame; will immediately understand the beauty and elegance of this most apt translation. But he will not attain the whole force and dignity, unless he also considers that the most artful embroidery with the needle was dedicated by the Hebrews to the service of the sanctuary; and that the proper and singular use of their work was, by the immediate prescript of the Divine law, applied in a certain part of the high priest's dress, and in the curtains of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exo.28.39">Exo 28:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.26.36">Exo 26:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.27.16">Exo 27:16</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="Eze.16.10">Eze 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.13.18">Eze 13:18</reference>. So that the psalmist may well be supposed to have compared the wisdom of the Divine Artificer particularly with that specimen of human art, whose dignity was through religion the highest, and whose elegance (<reference osisRef="Exo.35.30-Exo.35.35">Exo 35:30-35</reference>) was so exquisite, that the sacred writer seems to attribute it to a Divine inspiration." <div eID="gen23339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> In the lowest parts of the earth - The womb of the mother, thus expressed by way of delicacy.
entries.eb2f8570a54127dd10fb97460bc49196ba41e2f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> Thine eyes did see my substance - גלמי golmi, my embryo state - my yet indistinct mass, when all was wrapped up together, before it was gradually unfolded into the lineaments of man. "Some think," says Dr. Dodd, "that the allusion to embroidery is still carried on. As the embroiderer has still his work, pattern, or carton, before him, to which he always recurs; so, by a method as exact, revere all my members in continuance fashioned, i.e., from the rude embryo or mass they daily received some degree of figuration; as from the rude skeins of variously coloured silk or worsted, under the artificer's hands, there at length arises an unexpected beauty, and an accurate harmony of colcurs and proportions." <div eID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> And in thy book all my members were written - "All those members lay open before God's eyes; they were discerned by him as clearly as if the plan of them had been drawn in a book, even to the least figuration of the body of the child in the womb."
entries.8cbdead4ee59fb93de8df62f6f7cfa0915fc6c52: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23343" type="x-p"/> How precious also are thy thoughts - רעיך reeycha, thy cogitations; a Chaldaism, as before. <div eID="gen23343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> How great is the sum of them! - מה עצמו ראשיהם mah atsemu rasheyhem; How strongly rational are the heads or principal subjects of them! But the word may apply to the bones, עצמות atsamoth, the structure and uses of which are most curious and important.
entries.4b663f5e64cc55c1a1a18c15aebe2b9dd073a577: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23345" type="x-p"/> If I should count them - I should be glad to enumerate so many interesting particulars: but they are beyond calculation. <div eID="gen23345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23346" type="x-p"/> When I awake - Thou art my Governor and Protector night and day. <div eID="gen23346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23347" type="x-p"/> I am still with thee - All my steps in life are ordered by thee: I cannot go out of thy presence; I am ever under the influence of thy Spirit. <div eID="gen23347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23348" type="x-p"/> The subject, from the <reference osisRef="Psa.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference> to the <reference osisRef="Psa.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference> inclusive, might have been much more particularly illustrated, but we are taught, by the peculiar delicacy of expression in the Sacred Writings, to avoid, as in this case, the entering too minutely into anatomical details. I would, however, make an additional observation on the subject in the <reference osisRef="Psa.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>. I have already remarked the elegant allusion to embroidery, in the word רקמתי rukkamti, in the astonishing texture of the human body; all of which is said to be done in secret, בסתר bassether, in the secret place, viz., the womb of the mother, which, in the conclusion of the verse, is by a delicate choice of expression termed the lower parts of the earth. <div eID="gen23348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23349" type="x-p"/> The embryo state, גלם golem, has a more forcible meaning than our word substance amounts to. גלם galam signifies to roll or wrap up together; and expresses the state of the fetus before the constituent members were developed. The best system of modern philosophy allows that to semine masculino all the members of the future animal are contained; and that these become slowly developed or unfolded, in the case of fowls, by incubation; and in the case of the more perfect animals, by gestation in the maternal matrix. It is no wonder that, in considering these, the psalmist should cry out, How precious, or extraordinary, are thy thoughts! how great is the sum-heads or outlines, of them! The particulars are, indeed, beyond comprehension; even the heads - the general contents, of thy works; while I endeavor to form any tolerable notion of them, prevail over me - they confound my understanding, and are vastly too multitudinous for my comprehension.
entries.fd2f8b36c986328517b263aafa8dc605022b3979: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23350" type="x-p"/> Surely thou wilt slay the wicked - The remaining part of this Psalm has no visible connection with the preceding. I rather think it a fragment, or a part of some other Psalm. <div eID="gen23350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23351" type="x-p"/> Ye bloody men - אנשי דמים anshey damim, men of blood, men guilty of death.
entries.33221b0f5b422e219604038276d6871553285f9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23352" type="x-p"/> Thine enemies take thy name in vain - Bishop Horsley translates the whole verse thus: - "They have deserted me who are disobedient to thee; "They who are sworn to a rash purpose - thy refractory adversaries." <div eID="gen23352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23353" type="x-p"/> The original is obscure: but I cannot see these things in it. Some translate the Hebrew thus: "Those who oppose thee iniquitously seize unjustly upon thy cities;" and so almost all the Versions. The words, thus translated, may apply to Sanballat, Tobiah, and the other enemies of the returned Jews, who endeavored to drive them from the land, that they might possess the cities of Judea.
entries.2b9837157b53f2d148f26ca11b536e3a19ce1164: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23354" type="x-p"/> Do not I hate them - I hold their conduct in abomination.
entries.ea451c5cd384863e27ad7231ae32fc8a8934de32: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen23354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23355" type="x-p"/> With perfect hatred - Their conduct, their motives, their opposition to thee, their perfidy and idolatrous purposes, I perfectly abhor. With them I have neither part, interest, nor affection.
entries.103a5a83abe06ad91f7a5d8a283099f911db25d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen23355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23356" type="x-p"/> Search me, O God - Investigate my conduct, examine my heart, put me to the test, and entwine my thoughts.
entries.6f28fb6ff103818333e3c8e26499e8265792c67b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen23356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> If there be any wicked way - דרך עצב derech otseb: a way of idolatry or of error. Any thing false in religious principle; any thing contrary to piety to thyself, and love and benevolence to man. And he needed to offer such prayer as this, while filled with indignation against the ways of the workers of iniquities; for he who hates, utterly hates, the practices of any man, is not far from hating the man himself. It is very difficult "To hate the sin with all the heart, <div eID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> And yet the sinner love." <div eID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23359" type="x-p"/> Lead me in the way everlasting - בדרך עולם bederech olam, in the old way - the way in which our fathers walked, who worshipped thee, the infinitely pure Spirit, in spirit and in truth. Lead me, guide me, as thou didst them. We have ארח עולם orach olam, the old path, <reference osisRef="Job.22.15">Job 22:15</reference>. "The two words דרך derech and ארח orach, differ," says Bishop Horsley, "in their figurative senses: derech is the right way, in which a man ought to go; orach is the way, right or wrong, in which a man actually goes by habit." The way that is right in a man's own eyes is seldom the way to God.  <chapter eID="Ps.139"/> <div eID="gen23359" type="x-p"/>

entries.e9834275a346caa109af0c29424dd03f50f5cb58: <div eID="gen10271" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Adoration of the Omniscient and Omnipresent One</title> <div sID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> In this Aramaizing Psalm what the preceding Psalm says in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference> comes to be carried into effect, viz.: <hi type="italic">for Jahve is exalted and He seeth the lowly, and the proud He knoweth from afar</hi>. This Psalm has manifold points of contact with its predecessor. From a theological point of view it is one of the most instructive of the Psalms, and both as regards its contents and poetic character in every way worthy of David. But it is only inscribed לדוד because it is composed after the Davidic model, and is a counterpart to such Psalms as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> and to other Davidic didactic Psalms. For the addition למנצח neither proves its ancient Davidic origin, nor in a general way its origin in the period prior to the Exile, as Ps 74 for example shows, which was at any rate not composed prior to the time of the Chaldaean catastrophe. <div eID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> The Psalm falls into three parts: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13">Psa 139:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference>; the strophic arrangement is not clear. The first part celebrates the Omniscient and Omnipresent One. The poet knows that he is surrounded on all sides by God’s knowledge and His presence; His Spirit is everywhere and cannot be avoided; and His countenance is turned in every direction and inevitably, in wrath or in love. In the second part the poet continues this celebration with reference to the origin of man; and in the third part he turns in profound vexation of spirit towards the enemies of such a God, and supplicates for himself His proving and guidance. In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">Psa 139:4</reference> God is called <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference> <hi type="italic">El</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference> <hi type="italic">Eloha</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.21">Psa 139:21</reference> again <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference> again <hi type="italic">El</hi>. Strongly as this Psalm is marked by the depth and pristine freshness of its ideas and feeling, the form of its language is still such as is without precedent in the Davidic age. To all appearance it is the Aramaeo-Hebrew idiom of the post-exilic period pressed into the service of poetry. The Psalm apparently belongs to those Psalms which, in connection with a thoroughly classical character of form, bear marks of the influence which the Aramaic language of the Babylonian kingdom exerted over the exiles. This influence affected the popular dialect in the first instance, but the written language also did not escape it, as the Books of Daniel and Ezra show; and even the poetry of the Psalms is not without traces of this retrograde movement of the language of Israel towards the language of the patriarchal ancestral house. In the <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex</hi>. Ζαχαρίου is added to the τῷ Δαυίδ ψαλμός, and by a second hand ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ, which Origen also met with “in some copies.”
entries.a0dcfd623f1fb43613f32ba5cab23f2a9b5d88d4: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.7">Psa 139:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> The Aramaic forms in this strophe are the ἅπαξ λεγομ רע (ground-form רעי) in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, endeavour, desire, thinking, like רעוּת and רעיון in the post-exilic books, from רעה (רעא), <hi type="italic">cupere, cogitare</hi>; and the ἅπ. λεγ. רבע in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference>, equivalent to רבץ, a lying down, if רבעי be not rather an infinitive like בּלעי in <reference osisRef="Job.7.19">Job 7:19</reference>, since ארחי is undoubtedly not inflected from ארח, but, as being infinitive, like עברי in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.21">Deu 4:21</reference>, from ארח; and the verb ארח also, with the exception of this passage, only occurs in the speeches of Elihu (<reference osisRef="Job.34.8">Job 34:8</reference>), which are almost more strongly Aramaizing than the Book of Job itself. Further, as an Aramaizing feature we have the objective relation marked by <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in the expression בּנתּה לרעי, Thou understandest my thinking, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.11">Psa 135:11</reference>; Psa 136:19. The monostichic opening is after the Davidic style, e.g., <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Psa 23:1</reference></hi>. Among the prophets, Isaiah in particular is fond of such thematic introductions as we have here in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference></hi>. On ותּדע instead of ותּדעני vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>; the pronominal object stands once beside the first verb, or even beside the second (2Ki 9:25), instead of twice (Hitzig). The “me” is then expanded: sitting down, rising up, walking and lying, are the sum of human conditions or states. רעי is the totality or sum of the life of the spirit and soul of man, and דּרכי the sum of human action. The divine knowledge, as ותּדע says, is the result of the scrutiny of man. The poet, however, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference> uses the perfect throughout as a mood of that which is practically existing, because that scrutiny is a scrutiny that is never unexecuted, and the knowledge is consequently an ever-present knowledge. מרחוק is meant to say that He sees into not merely the thought that is fully fashioned and matured, but even that which is being evolved. זרית from זרה is combined by Luther (with Azulai and others) with זר, <hi type="italic">a wreath</hi> (from זרר, <hi type="italic">constringere, cingere</hi>), inasmuch as he renders: whether I walk or lie down, Thou art round about me (<hi type="italic">Ich gehe oder lige , so bistu umb mich</hi>). זרה ought to have the same meaning here, if with Wetzstein one were to compare the Arabic, and more particularly Beduin, <hi type="italic">drrâ , dherrâ</hi>, to protect; the notion of affording protection does not accord with this train of thought, which has reference to God’s omniscience: what ought therefore to be meant is a hedging round which secures its object to the knowledge, or even a protecting that places it in security against any exchanging, which will not suffer the object to escape it.<note placement="foot">This <hi type="italic">Verb. tert.</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">w et y</hi> is old, and the derivative <hi type="italic">dherâ</hi>, protection, is an elegant word; with reference to another derivative, <hi type="italic">dherwe</hi>, a wall of rock protecting one from the winds, vid., Job, at <reference osisRef="Job.24.7">Job 24:7</reference>, note. The II form (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi>) signifies to protect in the widest possible sense, e.g., (in <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi>, ii. 343 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), “[Arab.] <hi type="italic">drâ 'l - šâh</hi>, he protected the sheep (against being exchanged) by leaving a lock of wool upon their backs when they were shorn, by which they might be recognised among other sheep.”</note> <div eID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10275" type="x-p"/> The Arabic <hi type="italic">ḏrâ</hi>, to know, which is far removed in sound, is by no means to be compared; it is related to Arab. <hi type="italic">dr'</hi>, to push, urge forward, and denotes knowledge that is gained by testing and experimenting. But we also have no need of that Arab. <hi type="italic">ḏrâ</hi>, to protect, since we can remain within the range of the guaranteed Hebrew usage, inasmuch as זרה, to winnow, i.e., to spread out that which has been threshed and expose it to the current of the wind, in Arabic likewise <hi type="italic">ḏrrâ</hi>, (whence מזרה, <hi type="italic">midhrâ</hi>, a winnowing-fork, like רחת, <hi type="italic">racht</hi>, a winnowing-shovel), gives an appropriate metaphor. Here it is equivalent to: to investigate and search out to the very bottom; lxx, Symmachus, and Theodotion, ἐξιξηνίασας, after which the Italic renders <hi type="italic">investigasti</hi>, and Jerome <hi type="italic">eventilasti</hi>. הסכּין with the accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference> with עם: to enter into neighbourly, close, familiar relationship, or to stand in such relationship, with any one; cogn. שׁכן, Arab. <hi type="italic">skn</hi>. God is acquainted with all our ways not only superficially, but closely and thoroughly, as that to which He is accustomed. <div eID="gen10275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10276" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">Psa 139:4</reference> this omniscience of God is illustratively corroborated with כּי; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">Psa 139:4</reference></hi> has the value of a relative clause, which, however, takes the form of an independent clause. מלּה (pronounced by Jerome in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, §82, <hi type="italic">MALA</hi>) is an Aramaic word that has been already incorporated in the poetry of the Davidico-Salomonic age. כלּהּ signifies both all of it and every one. In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.5">Psa 139:5</reference> Luther has been misled by the lxx and Vulgate, which take צוּר in the signification <hi type="italic">formare</hi> (whence צוּרה, <hi type="italic">forma</hi>); it signifies, as the definition “behind and before” shows, to surround, encompass. God is acquainted with man, for He holds him surrounded on all sides, and man can do nothing, if God, whose confining hand he has lying upon him (<reference osisRef="Job.9.23">Job 9:23</reference>), does not allow him the requisite freedom of motion. Instead of דּעתּך (XX ἡ γνῶσίς σου) the poet purposely says in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference></hi> merely דּעת: a knowledge, so all-penetrating, all-comprehensive as God’s knowledge. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> reads פּליאה, but the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> פּלאיּה is supported by the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> פּלאי in Jdg 13:18, the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> of which there is not פּליא, but פּלי (the pausal form of an adjective פּלי, the feminine of which would be פּליּה). With ממּנּי the transcendence, with נשׂגּבה the unattainableness, and with להּ לא־אוּכל the incomprehensibleness of the fact of the omniscience of God is expressed, and with this, to the mind of the poet, coincides God’s omnipresence; for true, not merely phenomenal, knowledge is not possible without the immanence of the knowing one in the thing known. God, however, is omnipresent, sustaining the life of all things by His Spirit, and revealing Himself either in love or in wrath - what the poet styles His countenance. To flee from this omnipresence (מן, away from), as the sinner and he who is conscious of his guilt would gladly do, is impossible. Concerning the first אנּה, which is here accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, vid., on Psa 116:4.
entries.b6ba2d921ce3c7e6104d1c552677c67db427de32: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8-Ps.139.12">Psa 139:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen10276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10277" type="x-p"/> The future form אסּק, customary in the Aramaic, may be derived just as well from סלק (סלק), by means of the same mode of assimilation as in יסּב = יסבּב, as from נסק (נסק), which latter is certainly only insecurely established by <reference osisRef="Dan.6.24">Dan 6:24</reference>, להנסקה (cf. להנזקת, Ezr 4:22; הנפּק, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.2">Dan 5:2</reference>), since the <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>, as in להנעלה, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.3">Dan 4:3</reference>, can also be a compensation for the resolved doubling (vid., Bernstein in the <hi type="italic">Lexicon Chrestom. Kirschianae</hi>, and Levy <hi type="italic">s.v.</hi> נסק). אם with the simple future is followed by cohortatives (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>) with the equivalent אשּׂא among them: <hi type="italic">et si stratum facerem </hi>(<hi type="italic">mihi</hi>) <hi type="italic">infernum</hi> (accusative of the object as in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa 58:5</reference>), etc. In other passages the wings of the sun (Mal 4:2) and of the wind (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>) are mentioned, here we have the wings of the morning’s dawn. <hi type="italic">Pennae aurorae</hi>, Eugubinus observes (1548), <hi type="italic">est velocissimus aurorae per omnem mundum decursus</hi>. It is therefore to be rendered: If I should lift wings (נשׂא כנפים as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.16">Eze 10:16</reference>, and frequently) such as the dawn of the morning has, i.e., could I fly with the swiftness with which the dawn of the morning spreads itself over the eastern sky, towards the extreme west and alight there. Heaven and Hades, as being that which is superterrestrial and subterrestrial, and the east and west are set over against one another. אחרית ים is the extreme end of the sea (of the Mediterranean with the “isles of the Gentiles”). In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.10">Psa 139:10</reference> follows the apodosis: nowhere is the hand of God, which governs everything, to be escaped, for <hi type="italic">dextera Dei ubique est.</hi> ואמר (not ואמר, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.15">Eze 13:15</reference>), “therefore I spake,” also has the value of a hypothetical protasis: <hi type="italic">quodsi dixerim</hi>. אך and חשׁך belongs together: <hi type="italic">merae tenebrae</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>: Psa 39:6.); but ישׁוּפני is obscure. The signification secured to it of <hi type="italic">conterere, contundere</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job 9:17</reference>, which is followed by the lxx (Vulgate) καταπατήσει, is inappropriate to darkness. The signification <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi>, which may be deduced as possible from שׁאף, suits relatively better, yet not thoroughly well (why should it not have been יבלעני?). The signification <hi type="italic">obvelare</hi>, however, which one expects to find, and after which the Targum, Symmachus, Jerome, Saadia, and others render it, seems only to be guessed at from the connection, since שׁוּף has not this signification in any other instance, and in favour of it we cannot appeal either to נשׁף - whence נשׁף, which belongs together with נשׁב, נשׁם, and נפשׁ - or to עטף, the root of which is עת (עתה), or to צעף, whence צעיף, which does not signify to cover, veil, but according to Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍ‛f</hi>, to fold, fold together, to double. We must therefore either assign to ישׁוּפני the signification <hi type="italic">operiat me</hi> without being able to prove it, or we must put a verb of this signification in its place, viz., ישׂוּכני (Ewald) or יעוּפני (Böttcher), which latter is the more commendable here, where darkness (חשׁך, synon. עיפה, מעוּף) is the subject: and if I should say, let nothing but darkness cover me, and as night (the predicate placed first, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">Amo 4:13</reference>) let the light become about me, i.e., let the light become night that shall surround and cover me (בּעדני, poetic for בּעדי, like תּחתּני in 2 Sam. 22) -) -  the darkness would spread abroad no obscurity (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.28">Psa 105:28</reference>) that should extend beyond (מן) Thy piercing eye and remove me from Thee. In the word יאיר, too, the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> signification is not lost: the night would give out light from itself, as if it were the day; for the distinction of day and night has no conditioning influence upon God, who is above and superior to all created things (<hi type="italic">der Uebercreatürliche</hi>), who is light in Himself. The two כ are correlative, as e.g., in 1Ki 22:4. חשׁיכה (with a superfluous <hi type="italic">Jod</hi>) is an old word, but אורה (cf. Aramaic אורתּא) is a later one.
entries.81fa9f8c913b1f1df655bd4b7a350f9b52e14056: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.18">Psa 139:13-18</reference> <div eID="gen10277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10278" type="x-p"/> The fact that man is manifest to God even to the very bottom of his nature, and in every place, is now confirmed from the origin of man. The development of the child in the womb was looked upon by the Israelitish Chokma as one of the greatest mysteries, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>; and here the poet praises this coming into being as a marvellous work of the omniscient and omnipresent omnipotence of God. קנה here signifies <hi type="italic">condere</hi>; and סכך not: to cover, protect, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.22">Job 40:22</reference>, prop. to cover with network, to hedge in, but: to plait, interweave, viz., with bones, sinews, and veins, like שׂכך in Job 10:11. The reins are made specially prominent in order to mark the, the seat of the tenderest, most secret emotions, as the work of Him who trieth the heart and the reins. The προσευχή becomes in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference> the εὐχαριστία: I give thanks unto Thee that I have wonderfully come into being under fearful circumstances, i.e., circumstances exciting a shudder, viz., of astonishment (נוראות as in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.6">Psa 65:6</reference>). נפלה (= נפלא) is the passive to הפלה, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>; Psa 17:7. Hitzig regards נפליתה (Thou hast shown Thyself wonderful), after the lxx, Syriac, Vulgate, and Jerome, as the only correct reading; but the thought which is thereby gained comes indeed to be expressed in the following line, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference></hi>, which sinks down into tautology in connection with this reading. `otsem (collectively equivalent to עצמים, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>) is the bones, the skeleton, and, starting from that idea, more generally the state of being as a sum-total of elements of being. אשׁר, without being necessarily a conjunction (Ew. §333, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), attaches itself to the suffix of עצמי. רקּם, “to be worked in different colours, or also embroidered,” of the system of veins ramifying the body, and of the variegated colouring of its individual members, more particularly of the inward parts; perhaps, however, more generally with a retrospective conception of the colours of the outline following the undeveloped beginning, and of the forming of the members and of the organism in general.<note placement="foot">In the Talmud the egg of a bird or of a reptile is called מרקּמת, when the outlines of the developed embryo are visible in it; and likewise the mole (<hi type="italic">mola</hi>), when traces of human; organization can be discerned in it.</note> <div eID="gen10278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10279" type="x-p"/> The mother’s womb is here called not merely סתר (cf. Aeschylus’ <hi type="italic">Eumenides</hi>, 665: ἐν σκοτοισι νηδύος τεθραμμένη, and the designation of the place where the foetus is formed as “a threefold darkness’ in the Koran, <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. xxxix. 8), the <hi type="italic">ē</hi> of which is retained here in pause (vid., Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Lehrbuch</hi>, §298), but by a bolder appellation תּחתּיּות ארץ, the lowest parts of the earth, i.e., the interior of the earth (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>) as being the secret laboratory of the earthly origin, with the same retrospective reference to the first formation of the human body out of the dust of the earth, as when Job says,  <reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference> : “naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” -  שׁמּה, viz., εἰς τὴν γῆν τὴν μητέρα πάντων, Sir. 40:1. The interior of Hades is also called בּטן שׁאול in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>, Sir. 51:5. According to the view of Scripture the mode of Adam’s creation is repeated in the formation of every man, <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference>, cf. Job 33:4. The earth was the mother’s womb of Adam, and the mother’s womb out of which the child of Adam comes forth is the earth out of which it is taken.
entries.6ac8685cc820141ed6f40f67e0337663341bbfca: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19-Ps.139.21">Psa 139:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen10283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10284" type="x-p"/> And this God is by many not only not believed in and loved, but even hated and blasphemed! The poet now turns towards these enemies of God in profound vexation of spirit. The אם, which is conditional in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>, here is an optative <hi type="italic">o si</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.9">Psa 81:9</reference>; Psa 95:7. The expression תּקטל אלוהּ reminds one of the Book of Job, for, with the exception of our Psalm, this is the only book that uses the verb קטל, which is more Aramaic than Hebrew, and the divine name <hi type="italic">Eloah</hi> occurs more frequently in it than anywhere else. The transition from the optative to the imperative סוּרוּ is difficult; it would have been less so if the <hi type="italic">Waw copul</hi>. had been left out: cf. the easier expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.9">Psa 6:9</reference>; Psa 119:115. But we may not on this account seek to read יסוּרוּ, as Olshausen does. Everything here is remarkable; the whole Psalm has a characteristic form in respect to the language. מנּי is the ground-form of the overloaded ממּנּי, and is also like the Book of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>, cf. מנהוּ <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">Job 4:12</reference>, Psa 68:24. The mode of writing ימרוּך (instead of which, however, the Babylonian texts had יאמרוּך) is the same as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">2Sa 19:15</reference>, cf. in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9">2Sa 20:9</reference> the same melting away of the <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> into the preceding vowel in connection with אחז, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.40">2Sa 22:40</reference> in connection with אזּר, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Isa 13:20</reference> with אהל. Construed with the accusative of the person, אמר here signifies to declare any one, <hi type="italic">profiteri</hi>, a meaning which, we confess, does not occur elsewhere. But למזמּה (cf. למרמה, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>; the Targum: who swear by Thy name for wantonness) and the parallel member of the verse, which as it runs is moulded after <reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Exo 20:7</reference>, show that it has not to be read ימרוּך (Quinta: παρεπικρανάν σε). The form נשׁוּא, with <hi type="italic">Aleph otians</hi>, is also remarkable; it ought at least to have been written נשׂאוּ (cf. נרפּוּא, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">Eze 47:8</reference>) instead of the customary נשׂאוּ; yet the same mode of writing is found in the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">Jer 10:5</reference>, ינשׁוּא, it assumes a ground-form נשׂה (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>) = נשׂא, and is to be judged of according to אבוּא in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Isa 28:12</reference> [Ges. §23, 3, rem. 3]. Also one feels the absence of the object to נשׁוּא לשּׁוא. It is meant to be supplied according to the decalogue, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Exo 20:7</reference>, which certainly makes the alteration שׁמך (Böttcher, Olsh.) or זכרך (Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Isa 26:13</reference>), instead of עריך, natural. But the text as we now have it is also intelligible: the object to נשׂוא is derived from ימרוך, and the following עריך is an explanation of the subject intended in נשׂוא that is introduced subsequently. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.52">Psa 89:52</reference> proves the possibility of this structure of a clause. It is correctly rendered by Aquila ἀντίζηλοί σου, and Symmachus οἱ ἐναντίοι σου. ער, an enemy, prop. one who is zealous, a zealot (from עוּר, or rather עיר, = Arab. <hi type="italic">gâr , med . Je</hi>, ζηλοῦν, whence עיר, Arab. <hi type="italic">gayrat</hi> = קנאה), is a word that is guaranteed by <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">1Sa 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>, and as being an Aramaism is appropriate to this Psalm. The form תּקומם for מתּקומם has cast away the preformative <hi type="italic">Mem</hi> (cf. שׁפתּים and משׁפּתים, מקּרה in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.11">Deu 23:11</reference> for ממּקּרה); the suffix is to be understood according to Psa 17:7. <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> stands between יהוה and אשׂנה in order that the two words may not be read together (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.27.13">Job 27:13</reference>, and above <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>). התקוטט as in the recent Psa 119:158. The emphasis in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.22">Psa 139:22</reference></hi> lies on לי; the poet regards the adversaries of God as enemies of his own. תּכלית takes the place of the adjective: <hi type="italic">extremo</hi> (<hi type="italic">odio</hi>) <hi type="italic">odi eos</hi>. Such is the relation of the poet to the enemies of God, but without indulging any self-glorying.
entries.7e27551dfbfd44be8baedef4e4eb2b52a280a5bf: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23-Ps.139.24">Psa 139:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen10284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10285" type="x-p"/> He sees in them the danger which threatens himself, and prays God not to give him over to the judgment of self-delusion, but to lay bare the true state of his soul. The fact “Thou hast searched me,” which the beginning of the Psalm confesses, is here turned into a petitioning “search me.” Instead of רעים in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, the poet here says שׂרעפּים, which signifies branches (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">Eze 31:5</reference>) and branchings of the act of thinking (thoughts and cares, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.19">Psa 94:19</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> is epenthetic, for the first form is שׂעפּים, <reference osisRef="Job.4.13">Job 4:13</reference>; Job 20:2. The poet thus sets the very ground and life of his heart, with all its outward manifestations, in the light of the divine omniscience. And in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference> he prays that God would see whether any דּרך־עצב cleaves to him (בּי as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.24">1Sa 25:24</reference>), by which is not meant “a way of idols” (Rosenmüller, Gesenius, and Maurer), after <reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">Isa 48:5</reference>, since an inclination towards, or even apostasy to, heathenism cannot be an unknown sin; nor to a man like the writer of this Psalm is heathenism any power of temptation. דוך בּצע (Grätz) might more readily be admissible, but דוך עצב is a more comprehensive notion, and one more in accordance with this closing petition. The poet gives this name to the way that leads to the pain, torture, viz., of the inward and outward punishments of sin; and, on the other hand, the way along which he wishes to be guided he calls דּרך עולם, the way of endless continuance (lxx, Vulgate, Luther), not the way of the former times, after <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer 6:16</reference> (Maurer, Olshausen), which thus by itself is ambiguous (as becomes evident from <reference osisRef="Job.22.15">Job 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>), and also does not furnish any direct antithesis. The “everlasting way” is the way of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference>), the way of the righteous, which stands fast for ever and shall not “perish” (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.139"/> <div eID="gen10285" type="x-p"/>
